final_answer:
Merge sort works by repeatedly splitting a list into halves, recursively sorting each half, and then merging the two sorted halves back together. Merging involves comparing elements from each half and appending the smaller one to a new list. This continues until the entire list is sorted. Merge sort has a stable sort with O(n log n) time complexity.  

Merge sort is preferred over quicksort for linked lists because it doesn’t require random access to elements (like arrays), which linked lists don’t provide efficiently. Quicksort relies on partitioning around a pivot, which can be costly in linked lists due to the lack of direct indexing. Additionally, merge sort can be implemented with O(1) extra space when using the list itself for merging, making it more suitable.  

Merge sort also maintains the order of equal elements (stable), which can be important in certain applications. The predictable performance and lack of worst-case O(n²) behavior make it a safer choice for linked lists.
